pages.x: Russia was losing the war, and its people were hungry. At court the empress trusted Rasputin, a wandering holy man from Siberia who seemed able to ease her son's bleeding illness. In December 1916 nobles who blamed him for the empire's troubles poisoned him, shot him and threw him into a frozen river.

In February 1917 women queuing for bread in Petrograd went on strike, and the soldiers sent to stop the crowds joined them. Within days Tsar Nicholas II gave up the throne, ending three centuries of the Romanovs. A provisional government took over, but it kept on fighting the war.

Germany let Vladimir Lenin, the exiled leader of the Bolsheviks, travel home through its lands in a sealed train, hoping he would make trouble. He did. Promising peace, land and bread, his party won over workers and soldiers, and on 7 November 1917 its Red Guards took the Winter Palace almost without a fight.

Lenin made peace with Germany in March 1918, giving up Ukraine, Poland, Finland and the Baltic lands, about a third of the old empire's people. He closed the elected assembly when his party lost the vote, and his secret police, the Cheka, began a Red Terror against all opponents.

In July 1918, with anti-Bolshevik forces closing in, the Bolsheviks shot Nicholas, his wife, their five children and four servants in a cellar in Yekaterinburg. For decades rumours said the youngest daughter, Anastasia, had escaped; DNA tests have since shown that all the children died.

The Reds fought the Whites, armies of officers, monarchists and liberals backed by foreign troops, and peasant armies, nationalists and anarchists across the whole empire. Leon Trotsky built the Red Army and rode from front to front in an armoured train. War, terror, hunger and typhus killed millions before the Reds won.

pages.x: In December 1922 Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the republics of the Caucasus joined as the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the first state ruled by a communist party. Lenin was soon struck down by strokes and died in 1924, and Joseph Stalin, outmanoeuvring Trotsky, took his place.

The revolution created the Soviet Union, which lasted until 1991, and inspired communist parties and revolutions around the world, from China to Cuba. It promised equality, but brought one-party rule, terror and famine, and for much of the 20th century the world was split between its followers and its enemies.
